title: Small talk and rapport
summary: What Americans actually chat about in the first and last five minutes of an interview or coffee chat, and how to use it to build warmth. Interviewers often form a 'would I staff this person' impression before the case even starts.

blocks.title: Why the first five minutes matter
blocks.body: US interviews usually open with two to five minutes of light conversation before the case. It is not filler: interviewers are checking whether you are easy to talk to, curious, and calm, the 'airport test' of whether they would enjoy a delay with you. The goal is a short, genuine exchange, then a smooth handoff to business. Match their energy, keep answers brief, and ask one question back.

blocks.title: The sports calendar (what's 'in season')
rows: College football Saturdays; huge in the Midwest. Michigan vs Ohio State ('The Game') is late November
NFL regular season, Sundays plus Monday/Thursday nights; Thanksgiving Day games
NFL playoffs, then the Super Bowl on a Sunday in early-to-mid February (ads, parties)
NBA and NHL regular seasons; NBA All-Star weekend in February
March Madness: college basketball tournament, office bracket pools
NBA and NHL playoffs; Finals in June
MLB baseball; postseason and World Series in October
blocks.note: Exact dates shift yearly; check the league site if you plan to reference a game.

blocks.title: Safe, easy topics
items: Weekend plans or how the weekend went: keep it to one or two specifics, then ask theirs.
Weather and seasons, especially in the Midwest: first snow, a long winter, a great fall day.
Travel: a recent trip, a city they live in, office location they love.
Food: a local restaurant, coffee spot, or a dish you have been trying to cook.
Sports as a light reference, even if you only follow the big moments.
School life: a class you are enjoying, a club event, Ann Arbor in the fall.
Their path: how they ended up at the firm or in their practice area.

blocks.title: Topics to avoid or keep very light
items: Politics, elections, and current controversies, even if the interviewer brings them up.
Religion, and personal questions about family plans, age, or relationships.
Salary, bonuses, or what someone earns.
Complaints about your school, previous employer, or other firms.
Strong opinions on sensitive social issues or immigration policy.

blocks.title: You don't need to be a sports fan
blocks.body: Knowing what is in season is enough. 'I'm still learning American football, but the Big House on a Saturday was something else' is honest and invites them to explain. Asking a good question beats faking expertise. If they are a fan of a team, ask how the season is going; people enjoy being the expert.

blocks.title: Openers and transitions that work
items: Opener: 'How's your week going so far?' Then actually listen and respond to the detail.
Opener: 'Are you based in Chicago? I'm hoping to visit this fall. Anything I shouldn't miss?'
Bridge from your side: 'Good, thanks. Busy week with midterms, but I spent Saturday at the football game, which was a first.'
Transition to the case: 'I'm excited to dig in. Should we get started?'
Close: 'Thanks, this was fun. Good luck to the team this weekend.'

blocks.title: Showing curiosity
blocks.body: Americans read follow-up questions as interest. Use their detail: if they mention a ski trip, ask where and whether it was their first time. Avoid an interrogation: one question, a short reaction ('That sounds great'), and a bit about you. Share small personal details freely; Americans expect light self-disclosure. Mentioning your home city's food, a sport you follow (cricket counts), or a memorable job often sparks good questions.

blocks.title: Rapport norms: India vs US (tendencies)
rows: Often moves to business quickly in formal settings, or to family and background
Two to five minutes of light, personal-but-not-private talk
Weekend, sports in season, weather, travel, food
Family and marital questions can be ordinary
Family, age, and relationship questions usually avoided with strangers
First names right away, including partners

blocks.title: Small talk is not a test of trivia
blocks.body: Candidates sometimes over-prepare sports facts and sound scripted. The interviewer is not grading knowledge. A warm 30-second exchange beats a recited stat. Keep it short when the interviewer seems rushed, and let them decide when to move to the case.

in_a_case: First two minutes of a case interview: a short, warm exchange, then let the interviewer move to the prompt. Do not launch the case unprompted.
Coffee chats: spend the first few minutes on their path or something you share (your school, a home country, a city) before asking about the firm.
Fit stories land better when they include small human details, the same instinct as good small talk.
End-of-interview questions are a rapport moment: ask about their experience, not facts you could find online.
In a sports or media case (e.g., ticketing, streaming rights), knowing the season calendar helps you reason about seasonality.

flashcards.back: Regular season September to early January; playoffs in January; Super Bowl on a Sunday in early-to-mid February.
The college basketball tournament, mid-March to early April; offices often run bracket pools.
Late March to October, with the World Series in late October.

flashcards.front: What is 'The Game' in Ann Arbor?
flashcards.back: Michigan vs Ohio State football, played late November; Michigan Stadium ('The Big House') holds over 100,000.
Weekend plans, weather and seasons, travel or food (also sports in season).
Politics, religion, and pay (also family plans, age, health).

flashcards.front: How long is typical pre-interview small talk?
flashcards.back: About two to five minutes; the interviewer usually decides when to move on.
Ask one follow-up on a detail they mentioned, react briefly, then share a small detail about yourself.
